Newborn Care

Why babies rub their eyes

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Eye rubbing often goes with tiredness, but the surrounding signs matter. Check whether your baby is comfortable and whether there is redness, watering, discharge, pain or a change in how they look at you.

Start with the pattern around the rubbing

Babies often bring their hands toward their face, and a brief rub does not by itself mean there is a problem. It may happen with sleepiness, ordinary movement or an uncomfortable eye. Notice whether it affects one eye or both, whether it happens mainly before sleep, and whether the baby settles afterward. Look for redness, watering, discharge or difficulty opening the eye.

A baby cannot explain the difference between itching, pain and blurred vision. Persistent or vigorous rubbing therefore deserves attention even if the eye looks normal between episodes. It is not useful to treat the movement as deliberate disobedience or attention-seeking. Comfort and gentle redirection can help while you work out whether there is an underlying cause.

Tiredness is common, but sleep needs depend on age

Rubbing alongside yawning, looking away and fussiness may be a cue to offer a calm opportunity for sleep. You can reduce stimulation and follow your baby’s usual settling routine. Falling asleep afterward supports tiredness as one possibility, but does not prove that irritation or another concern is absent, particularly if rubbing keeps returning when the baby is rested.

The often-quoted twelve to sixteen hours of sleep in twenty-four hours applies to babies aged four to twelve months and includes naps. Newborn patterns differ and sleep is broken around feeding and care. Do not force a fixed schedule or delay necessary feeds to reach a number. For sleep, use a firm, flat surface and place the baby on their back, with their face uncovered.

Dust, dryness and allergies can irritate the eyes

Dry air, smoke, dust, sand, soap and other irritants can make an eye uncomfortable. Pollen, dust mites, mould or pet dander can trigger allergic symptoms in a susceptible child. Itchiness with watery redness may suggest allergy, but rubbing does not establish it. Allergy is not the default explanation for eye symptoms in a very young infant.

Notice whether symptoms follow an exposure, such as a dusty room or a visit with a pet, and remove an obvious irritant where possible. Do not spray cleaning products near the baby to solve the problem. An allergy assessment may be useful for recurrent symptoms, but ask a clinician before using medicated eye drops or antihistamines in a baby. Pain or marked light sensitivity needs a different level of attention.

Infection and blocked tear drainage can look similar

Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the membrane over the white of the eye and inner eyelids. Viral or bacterial infection can cause redness, watering, discharge or crusted lashes; a recent cold or contact with someone with red eyes may be relevant. Allergy can also inflame this surface. The symptoms overlap, so appearance alone does not reliably determine which medicine is needed.

A blocked tear duct can make an infant’s eye watery or sticky because tears do not drain normally. This is different from assuming every discharge is an infection. A professional can check the cause and demonstrate any recommended care. Antibiotics may be appropriate for a particular infection, but do not treat a virus or allergy and do not themselves open a blocked tear duct.

Consider vision concerns without diagnosing eye strain

A child with a vision problem may rub their eyes, but most rubbing is not enough to diagnose poor vision. Refractive errors affect how the eye focuses; cataracts affect the clarity of the lens. Both are examples of conditions an examination can detect. It is misleading to describe a baby’s eyes simply as overworked muscles or to assume that rubbing will reveal every vision difficulty.

Eye screening starts at birth and continues during infancy and childhood. By around three months, most babies can make steady eye contact and follow an object. Frequent inward crossing or outward drifting after about four months should be discussed with a clinician. Concerns at an earlier age also matter. A white or grey appearance in a pupil, a new abnormal eye movement or apparent difficulty seeing needs prompt assessment.

Teething should not explain away an eye problem

Teething can bring sore gums, increased chewing, drooling and fretfulness. Babies may rub their face or ears during the same period. However, the idea that an upper tooth routinely causes a painful or inflamed eye is not a reliable explanation. Check eye symptoms on their own merits rather than waiting for a tooth to emerge.

For gum discomfort, a suitable teething ring cooled in the refrigerator may help; follow its instructions and keep it clean. Do not freeze it or tie it around the neck. If pain medicine is needed, ask about an appropriate product and dose for the baby’s age and weight. Pain relief should not delay assessment of a red, persistently watery or painful eye.

Offer gentle care and avoid adding irritation

Wash your hands before and after touching the eye area, and keep the baby’s nails short and smooth. While they are awake, try comfort or an age-appropriate toy to redirect rubbing. Loose mittens are not a treatment for an eye condition and should not replace checking the cause; discuss any garment used to prevent scratching with the baby’s care team.

For crust on the eyelashes, a clinician may recommend gentle external cleaning with cooled boiled water and a fresh clean pad for each eye. Wipe the lashes without pressing on the eyeball. Do not share towels or washcloths when infection is possible. Avoid tea, breast milk, homemade mixtures, leftover prescriptions or someone else’s eye drops. Use prescribed drops only as directed for this baby.

Handle a suspected foreign body or splash safely

If loose dust or sand may have entered the eye, clean water can help rinse it away. Do not sweep a cloth, finger or cotton swab across the eyeball or try to dig under a baby’s eyelid. Seek prompt help if you cannot rinse it out, the baby will not open the eye, or watering and distress continue. Do not attempt to remove an object that appears embedded or has pierced the eye.

A chemical splash needs immediate action. Start gentle rinsing with plenty of clean, non-hot water and keep rinsing while getting emergency medical advice; NHS guidance recommends at least twenty minutes. Do not delay rinsing to look for a special solution, and do not add another chemical to neutralise it. Take the product container or its details to the medical team if this can be done without delaying care.

Know when to get an eye assessment

A baby younger than thirty days with red, sticky eyes needs urgent medical assessment. At any age, significant pain, marked swelling, severe redness, light sensitivity, an injury or an apparent change in sight needs urgent care. A baby who is unusually sleepy, feeding poorly or otherwise unwell should also be assessed. Chemical exposure or a penetrating injury is an emergency.

For mild rubbing without other symptoms, observe the pattern and offer appropriate rest and comfort. Arrange a visit if it persists, repeatedly affects one eye or worries you. Explain when it started, any exposure and whether feeding, sleep or visual behaviour has changed. You do not need to wait until six months of age, or until obvious discharge develops, to ask for help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pediatric eye guidance recommends screening from infancy and assessment of persistent symptoms or concerns about sight.

Infant red-eye care depends on the cause; newborn conjunctivitis and eye injuries need prompt attention rather than routine home treatment.

How BeMama can help

Notice when rubbing happens and what accompanies it. A short note can help at an appointment; do not provoke symptoms or delay urgent care to record them.

When to seek help

Red, sticky eyes in a baby under thirty days need urgent assessment. Chemical splashes, embedded objects, significant pain or apparent vision changes need urgent or emergency eye care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Rubbing alone does not identify the cause.
  • Use age-appropriate sleep expectations.
  • Do not dismiss an inflamed eye as teething.
  • Clean lashes gently without wiping across the eyeball.
  • Vision concerns deserve attention at any age.

Frequently asked questions

Does every eye rub mean my baby needs a nap?

No. Tiredness is one possibility, especially with yawning or fussiness, but irritation and other eye problems can also cause rubbing. Look at the whole pattern and any additional symptoms.

Do all babies need twelve to sixteen hours of sleep?

That range applies to ages four to twelve months, including naps. Newborn sleep patterns differ. Do not use a single sleep target to delay feeds or ignore persistent eye symptoms.

Could my baby have an eye allergy?

Possibly, but rubbing does not diagnose one. Itchy, watery eyes and an exposure pattern may help a clinician assess the cause. Do not assume allergy in a very young baby or start medicated drops without advice.

Does sticky discharge always mean an infection?

No. A blocked tear duct can also cause watering or discharge. A professional can distinguish the possibilities and explain whether cleaning, other care or a medicine is needed.

Can teething explain a red or painful eye?

It should not be used as that explanation without assessment. Teething commonly affects the gums and chewing behaviour; persistent redness, pain or watering deserves attention as an eye symptom.

Should I ignore rubbing as a bad habit?

No. A baby is not deliberately misbehaving. Gentle redirection can reduce rubbing, but frequent or forceful rubbing may signal discomfort and should not simply be ignored.

Can I wipe a speck from the eyeball with a cloth?

Do not wipe across the eyeball or dig for a particle. Gentle rinsing with clean water may remove loose material. An embedded object, injury, persistent distress or inability to open the eye needs urgent help.

Do antibiotic drops help every red eye?

No. They do not treat viral or allergic conjunctivitis, and they do not open a blocked tear duct. Use a prescribed medicine only for the baby and condition for which it was supplied.

When are red, sticky eyes urgent in a newborn?

A baby under thirty days with red, sticky eyes needs urgent medical assessment. Do not wait several days for home cleaning to work.

Should I wait until six months to mention a vision concern?

No. Screening begins earlier, and a concern about sight, eye alignment or pupil appearance should be raised when you notice it. The clinician can decide whether a specialist examination is needed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
